title: SVO Word Order (Subjek + Predikat + Objek)
explanation: Standard Indonesian follows Subject-Verb-Object order with no verb conjugation for tense or person. Time words clarify when an action happens.
example: Saya membaca buku setiap malam.
example_translation: I read a book every night.

title: Negation: tidak vs. bukan
explanation: Use 'tidak' before verbs and adjectives (tidak makan, tidak mahal). Use 'bukan' before nouns and noun phrases (bukan guru, bukan buku saya).
example: Dia bukan dokter; dia tidak bekerja di rumah sakit.
example_translation: He is not a doctor; he does not work at a hospital.

title: Aspect & Time Markers (sudah / belum / sedang / akan)
explanation: Indonesian verbs do not change form for tense. Place 'sudah' (already), 'belum' (not yet), 'sedang' (currently), or 'akan' (will) directly before the verb.
example: Saya sudah makan, tetapi adik belum makan.
example_translation: I have already eaten, but younger sibling has not eaten yet.

title: Core Location Prepositions (di / ke / dari)
explanation: Use 'di' for location (at/in), 'ke' for destination (to), and 'dari' for origin (from). Always write a space between the preposition and place noun (di rumah, not dirumah).
example: Saya pergi ke kampus dari rumah.
example_translation: I go to campus from home.

title: Inclusive 'kita' vs. Exclusive 'kami'
explanation: Both mean 'we', but 'kita' includes the person you are speaking to, whereas 'kami' excludes the listener.
example: Kami berangkat sekarang. Sampai jumpa, semoga kita bertemu lagi!
example_translation: We (excluding you) are leaving now. See you, hope we (all) meet again!

title: Noun + Modifier Order (Head-Initial)
explanation: Adjectives, possessives, and demonstratives ('ini' this, 'itu' that) come AFTER the noun they modify.
example: Buku baru saya itu sangat menarik.
example_translation: That new book of mine is very interesting.

title: Yes/No Questions with 'Apakah'
explanation: Place 'Apakah' at the start of a declarative sentence to form a polite yes/no question. In casual speech, rising intonation alone is common.
example: Apakah Anda tinggal di Jakarta?
example_translation: Do you live in Jakarta?

title: Existential 'ada' (There is / Have)
explanation: Use 'ada' to express existence ('there is/are') or presence. In informal speech, it can also mean 'to have'.
example: Di meja ada dua gelas air.
example_translation: On the table there are two glasses of water.

title: Relative & Focus Marker 'yang'
explanation: Use 'yang' ('that/which/who') to introduce descriptive clauses or emphasize a specific adjective.
example: Pelajar yang rajin akan cepat maju.
example_translation: Students who are diligent will progress quickly.

title: Reduplication for Plurals (Kata Ulang)
explanation: Doubling a noun (buku-buku, teman-teman) indicates explicit plurality or variety. Do not double the noun when a number or 'banyak' already precedes it.
example: Anak-anak bermain di taman, dan ada tiga kucing.
example_translation: The children play in the park, and there are three cats.

title: Intransitive Prefix 'ber-'
explanation: The prefix 'ber-' forms intransitive verbs meaning 'to have', 'to wear', or 'to perform an activity' (berjalan, berbicara, belajar).
example: Mereka berbicara tentang rencana liburan.
example_translation: They are talking about vacation plans.

title: Active Transitive Prefix 'meN-'
explanation: The 'meN-' prefix creates active transitive verbs. Its nasal sound assimilates to the root's first letter, and initial p/t/k/s normally drops (tulis → menulis, baca → membaca).
example: Ibu memasak sup dan ayah membaca koran.
example_translation: Mother cooks soup and father reads the newspaper.

title: Passive Voice Prefix 'di-'
explanation: Replace 'meN-' with 'di-' (written without a space before the verb!) to form the 3rd-person passive voice, optionally followed by 'oleh' (by).
example: Buku ini ditulis oleh penulis terkenal.
example_translation: This book was written by a famous author.

title: Suffix '-nya' (Possessive & Definite Marker)
explanation: Attach '-nya' to a noun to mean 'his/her/its' or 'the (specific/known)'. On adjectives or verbs, it can nominalize the word.
example: Rumahnya dekat pasar, dan udaranya sejuk.
example_translation: His/her house is near the market, and the air is cool.

title: Comparatives & Superlatives (lebih / paling / ter-)
explanation: Use 'lebih + adj + daripada' for 'more ... than', and 'paling + adj' or prefix 'ter-' for 'the most ...'.
example: Kereta lebih cepat daripada bus, tetapi pesawat paling cepat.
example_translation: Trains are faster than buses, but planes are the fastest.

title: Accidental & Stative Prefix 'ter-'
explanation: Besides superlatives, 'ter-' on verbs expresses accidental/unintentional actions or a resulting state (terbuka = open, tertidur = fell asleep).
example: Pintu kelas terbuka karena angin kencang.
example_translation: The classroom door opened because of the strong wind.

title: Abstract Noun Circumfixes 'ke-...-an' & 'peN-...-an'
explanation: 'ke-...-an' forms state/quality nouns (kesehatan = health, kebebasan = freedom), while 'peN-...-an' forms process nouns (pendidikan = education, penelitian = research).
example: Pendidikan dan kesehatan adalah kunci kemajuan.
example_translation: Education and health are the keys to progress.

title: Causative & Benefactive Suffix '-kan'
explanation: Adding '-kan' to a verb often makes it causative ('make something become X': menjelaskan = make clear/explain) or benefactive ('do X for someone').
example: Guru menjelaskan materi baru kepada siswa.
example_translation: The teacher explained the new material to the students.

title: Concessive & Result Connectors
explanation: Use 'walaupun/meskipun' (although) to introduce contrast, 'sehingga' (so that/resulting in) for consequence, and 'namun' (however) at the start of a formal clause.
example: Walaupun hujan deras, acara tetap berlangsung sehingga semua peserta puas.
example_translation: Although it rained heavily, the event still took place so all participants were satisfied.

title: Common Noun Classifiers (Kata Penggolong)
explanation: Use 'orang' for people (tiga orang guru), 'ekor' for animals (dua ekor kucing), and 'buah' for general objects/fruits (sebuah buku).
example: Saya membeli sebuah kamus dan dua buah apel.
example_translation: I bought one dictionary and two apples.
